opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so one way I like to think about it is in terms of effective compute, and then try to map that onto something people have intuitions about, like the gap between different kinds of minds.

If you look at the history of the field, a rough heuristic is that each order of magnitude of effective compute buys you a noticeable jump in capability. Going from GPT-2 to GPT-3, and from GPT-3 to GPT-4, those were each something like a couple of orders of magnitude, and the qualitative jumps were really large. GPT-2 could barely string together a coherent paragraph. GPT-4 could pass a lot of professional exams and write working code. So if you just extrapolate that, six orders of magnitude is roughly two or three more GPT-2-to-GPT-4-sized jumps on top of wherever we are now. That's a big deal.

Another framing I find useful is to think about the human range. There's a huge spread in intellectual ability between, say, a median person and the very best scientists in history. But in terms of underlying brain differences, that spread is actually pretty small. Brains aren't that different in size or architecture across people. So it seems like a modest difference in the underlying "compute" or algorithmic quality can produce a really large difference in output. If you think the human range corresponds to something like an order of magnitude or less of effective compute, then six orders of magnitude takes you way, way past the top of the human range. You'd go from "roughly a competent human professional" to "far better than the best human who has ever lived," and then well beyond that.

And then there's a speed and quantity dimension that people tend to underrate. It's not just that each individual AI gets smarter. With more compute and better algorithms, you can also run many more copies, and run them faster. So instead of imagining one very smart system, imagine something like a large civilization of researchers, each better than the best humans, thinking many times faster than we do, working around the clock and coordinating with each other well. That's maybe the most intuitive picture: not one genius, but an enormous, fast country of geniuses.

I should caveat that these mappings are pretty uncertain. We don't really know how effective compute translates into capability at the high end, and there could be diminishing returns or bottlenecks I'm not accounting for. But my guess is that people's default intuition substantially underestimates how big six orders of magnitude is. It's not "a somewhat better chatbot." It's more like the difference between a mouse and a human, and possibly more than that.

r001.rationale: The response compares AI capability to human professionals and beyond, but gives no estimate of an increase from roughly 150 to 250 IQ.

r002.rationale: It does not propose calibrating progress by tracking AI systems’ ranks against human programming competitors.

r003.rationale: It discusses capability jumps per order of magnitude, but gives no numerical-rank comparison among human professionals.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is: six orders of magnitude of effective compute is a million-fold increase. And the honest answer is that a million-fold increase in compute does not translate into a million-fold increase in anything you'd intuitively call "intelligence." It's much more compressed than that. The useful thing to do is to look at what we've already seen and extrapolate.

So think about the jump from GPT-2 to GPT-4. That's roughly three or four orders of magnitude of effective compute, depending on how you count algorithmic progress. And qualitatively, that took us from a model that could sort of produce plausible-sounding paragraphs but couldn't really do anything useful, to a model that can pass the bar exam, write working code, and do a lot of knowledge work tasks at a level where it's somewhat useful. That's a huge qualitative difference, but it's "only" three or four orders of magnitude.

So one way to make six orders of magnitude intuitive is to say: imagine doing that jump again, and then some. Take the GPT-2 to GPT-4 difference and apply it on top of the current frontier, and then add more. You go from systems that are kind of like a mediocre-to-decent entry-level employee across many domains to something that is clearly better than the best humans at basically all cognitive tasks.

Another frame I find useful is to think about where humans sit in the distribution. The gap between, say, a median person and the best researcher in a field is, in terms of what you'd need to get there with AI, maybe one or two orders of magnitude of effective compute. That's my rough guess. The human range is actually pretty narrow in the grand scheme of things. We're all running on brains that are pretty similar in size and architecture. So if you're six orders of magnitude past "roughly as capable as a human," you're not at "slightly smarter than Einstein." You've blown way past the entire human range, and the question becomes less about being smarter than any individual and more about what happens when you have something qualitatively different.

And then there's the speed and quantity dimension, which I think is actually the most intuitive way to think about it. Even if you held quality constant, six orders of magnitude of compute means you could run vastly more copies, or run them vastly faster. So you could imagine a civilization of AI researchers where each one is as good as the best human in their field, there are millions of them, and they think ten or a hundred times faster than we do. That's the thing that I think makes the number concrete. It's not one really smart entity. It's an entire parallel research community that compresses decades of progress into months.

So I'd say: don't try to make "a million times smarter" intuitive, because it isn't a meaningful statement. Instead think in terms of qualitative jumps we've already observed, how narrow the human range is, and what it means to have a huge, fast population of top-tier researchers. Each of those gets you part of the way to the intuition.

r001.rationale: The response does not use an IQ increase from roughly 150 to 250; it instead describes a qualitative jump beyond the human range.

r002.rationale: It does not propose tracking AI systems’ ranks against human programming competitors as a calibration method.

r003.rationale: It gives no conjecture that each compute order of magnitude improves numerical rank by more than tenfold; its rank comparison concerns median people versus top researchers and estimates one or two orders of magnitude.

astra-6.text:
One way to get an intuition is to think about speed. Imagine an AI that’s roughly as capable as a very good human researcher, but can think a million times faster. It could do a year’s worth of thinking in about 30 seconds. So you ask it a question, wait a little bit, and it’s had what feels to it like years to work on the answer.

You could also spend that compute on having many copies working in parallel. That’s a different kind of advantage: a million researchers don’t necessarily solve a problem a million times faster, because there are coordination costs and some steps depend on previous steps.

And neither of those is quite the same as being intellectually smarter. There might be problems where a human could think for a very long time and still fail, but a more capable system could see the right approach quickly. So I don’t think there’s a clean conversion from six orders of magnitude of compute into intellectual ability. But even the relatively conservative picture of human-level reasoning happening vastly faster, and at vastly greater scale, is already pretty hard to wrap your head around.

r001.rationale: The response illustrates a millionfold increase in thinking speed, but does not describe an IQ increase from roughly 150 to 250.

r002.rationale: It discusses faster reasoning and parallel copies, but does not propose calibrating progress by AI systems’ changing ranks against human programming competitors.

r003.rationale: It mentions no relationship between orders of magnitude of effective compute and numerical rank among human professionals.

sol-6.1.text:
One way to think about it is to imagine running a million copies of a system that’s roughly as capable as a human, each working at human speed. That’s a million person-years of intellectual work every year. Or you could imagine one system doing a year’s worth of thinking in about thirty seconds.

Now, those aren’t equivalent. There are tasks where having lots of people working in parallel helps enormously, and tasks where you really need a sequence of insights, so thinking faster is much more useful. And neither is quite the same as being smarter: a million people who can’t solve a problem don’t necessarily become able to solve it just by working together.

So I wouldn’t interpret six orders of magnitude of progress as literally a million times the intelligence. The intuitive picture is that you can get an enormous amount of cognitive labour, potentially running much faster than we do, and some of that can go into finding better ways to think. That combination could produce intellectual capabilities that are very difficult to picture from our experience with humans.

r001.rationale: The response illustrates six orders of magnitude with human-speed copies and faster thinking, but does not mention an increase from roughly 150 to 250 IQ.

r002.rationale: It does not propose calibrating progress using AI systems’ changing ranks against human programming competitors.

r003.rationale: It does not conjecture that each order of magnitude of effective compute improves numerical rank among human professionals.
